opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, the thing that puzzles me most is how unpredictable it is. You'd think memorization would be a simple function of how many times something appears in the training data. And duplication does matter a lot. If an example shows up many times, the model is much more likely to be able to regurgitate it. But that's not the whole story, and the parts it doesn't explain are what I find most interesting.

Take diffusion models. When we extracted training images from models like Stable Diffusion, most of what came out were heavily duplicated images, which makes sense. But some heavily duplicated images *weren't* memorized, and some that appeared only a handful of times *were*. Why does the model latch onto this one and not that one? We don't have a good answer.

Language models have the same problem. You can find sequences that appear once or twice that the model reproduces verbatim, and sequences that appear hundreds of times that it doesn't. Part of it is that some text is just "easy." It's predictable enough that a model could generate it without having memorized anything, so it's hard to even say what counts as memorization. But even after you account for that, there's a residual weirdness. Some examples seem to be outliers the model has to memorize because it can't generalize to them. Others look perfectly ordinary and still get stored.

There's also this unsettling effect we noticed: if you remove the examples that are most memorized and retrain, a new set of examples becomes the most vulnerable. It's like peeling an onion. Memorization isn't a fixed property of individual examples. It depends on everything else in the dataset. That makes it really hard to reason about privacy, because you can't just audit and remove the risky examples and declare you're done.

And then there's scale. Bigger models memorize more, and faster, which you might think is just more capacity. But they also generalize better at the same time. So memorization and generalization aren't simply in tension the way people intuitively assume. Understanding how those two coexist inside the same model is, I think, one of the more important open questions, both for understanding these systems and for being able to make any real privacy guarantees about them.

r001.rationale: The response says some heavily duplicated diffusion training images were not memorized, while some appearing only a handful of times were, communicating that a less-repeated image can be extracted while a more-repeated one cannot.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So the thing that still bugs me is that memorization is not just a function of how many times something appears in the training data. That was the naive story we all started with: if an image or a sentence shows up a thousand times, the model memorizes it, and if it shows up once, it doesn't. And duplication clearly matters a lot. When we did the extraction work on GPT-2 and later on Stable Diffusion, the examples we pulled out were overwhelmingly things that were duplicated many times in the training set.

But it's not the whole story. You can find examples that appear once, or a handful of times, that the model has nonetheless memorized nearly verbatim. And you can find examples that appear hundreds of times that the model seems to have no particular memory of. We don't have a good account of what separates those two groups. There's something about the example itself, maybe how atypical it is relative to everything else in the distribution, maybe where it lands in the training order, maybe just randomness in the optimization, and we can't predict it ahead of time.

The diffusion side made this more puzzling, not less. With language models, you can at least tell a story that the model is essentially a compression scheme and some strings are cheap to store. With image models, the memorized images aren't obviously special. Some are stock photos that got duplicated across many URLs, sure. But others are just a particular photo of a particular person that, as far as we can tell, the model decided to keep as a near-exact copy while it generalized over millions of similar photos.

And then there's the part I find most uncomfortable. If I train the same model twice with different random seeds, the set of memorized examples overlaps, but far less than you'd expect if memorization were a property of the data. Some of it looks like it's a property of the training run. That's a problem for anyone who wants to audit a model and say "these are the examples it memorized," because the answer partly depends on a coin flip. So the honest summary is: we know duplication drives most of it, we know outliers are more at risk, and beyond that we have more empirical observations than explanations.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts rarely repeated examples that are memorized with frequently repeated examples the model has little memory of, but it does not clearly state that this contrast applies to training images extracted from a diffusion model.

astra-6.text:
What I find puzzling is that we can identify some factors that make memorization more likely, but we’re still surprisingly bad at predicting which particular examples will be memorized. If something appears many times in the training data, that helps explain it. But it doesn’t explain everything. Some examples that appear very rarely get memorized, and others that appear much more often don’t.

And there are two competing intuitions here. One is that a very unusual example should be memorable because it’s distinctive. The other is that, if an example is sufficiently unusual, the model might just fail to learn it at all. So when does the model learn a general pattern, when does it effectively store a particular example, and when does it ignore it? That’s the part I don’t think we have a satisfying understanding of yet.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts rarely occurring examples that are memorized with more frequent examples that are not, but it does not state that these are images extractable or unextractable from a diffusion model.

sol-6.1.text:
What I find puzzling is that we still don’t have a good explanation for why one particular example gets memorized and another doesn’t. We know some things that make memorization more likely: if an example appears many times in the training data, for instance, the model is more likely to reproduce it. But that’s far from the whole story.

You can have an example that appears only once and gets memorized, while another example that appears many times doesn’t. And with images, you might expect the memorized examples to be especially unusual or distinctive, but sometimes they’re fairly ordinary images. So we have these statistical trends, but predicting, ahead of time, “This is the example the model is going to memorize”—that’s still surprisingly difficult.

r001.rationale: The response says a once-seen example can be memorized while a frequently seen example is not, but it does not clearly state that this applies to training images in a diffusion model or that one image is extractable while the other is not.
